answer: Moving forty marker posts and paying 18,200 in bribes to the steward is what a false boundary costs, and the forgery still fails at the first inspection. The steward numbers a post for every row end and writes each number in the register beside the row's name. A copper post planted in the night carries no number at all: the steward checks the post against the canyon register at the row end, and a post whose number the register never issued is pulled out at once, while the thread map in the estate office is kept for ten years, so a row whose post was never numbered loses its edge.
